purpose: Consolidate preliminary source-QC findings into teacher sign-off workflow, without implying academic certification

originalSource.researchBasis: Compiled exclusively from V235 and V237–V248 original source-review records already merged; no claim of new direct textbook scan in V249

accounting.cognitiveMetadataClarification: V237 candidateCognitive records question-level demand; V249 observedCognitive preserves that field while officialPrintedCognitive is independently sourced from V224 printed framework.

triageDefinitions.SOURCE_LEVEL_ASSESSMENT_CONCERN: Question stem/options or numeric assumptions are not sufficient for an unambiguous scored result. Preserve original for discussion; repair via separately authored and teacher-approved substitute or formally exclude.
triageDefinitions.COMPULSORY_SOLUTION_QUALIFICATION: Original may remain, but the teacher explanation/diagram must explicitly state scientific boundary, model or process conditions before assessed publication.
triageDefinitions.OPTIONAL_TEACHER_NOTE: Optional teaching clarity or numerical-constant note; not evidence that the original publisher stem is defective.
triageDefinitions.SLO_ADJUDICATION: Authentic candidate SLO/cognitive level is not approval. A missing direct match or cognitive mismatch must be resolved against the official framework before graded use.

entries.sourceReasonReference: The source supplies a physically appropriate approximation criterion, but ideal behaviour is also aided by sufficiently high temperature and weak intermolecular effects.

entries.publisherStemConcern: competing thermodynamic-process classifications in source scenario
entries.sourceReasonReference: Ideal flask supports negligible heat transfer (adiabatic); nearly fixed volume of contained liquid and rigid container also supports isochoric classification. Those categories are not mutually exclusive, and 'due to' is underspecified.

entries.publisherStemConcern: physical boundary and process not specified; single answer unjustified
entries.sourceReasonReference: Fasting alone does not determine whether a selected metabolism/body system follows constant temperature, constant pressure, constant volume, or zero-heat-transfer conditions. The system boundary and constraints are unstated.
Rigid container eliminates boundary P-dV work; apply First Law with the usual heat-input interpretation of symbol Q. Other work modes are not specified.
The printed constant pressure and initial/final volumes define positive work done by gas using W=P(V_f−V_i), with SI pressure and volume units. Printed options include the consistent result.
In the listed phase-change alternatives, transfer from solid to gas increases entropy of the material; freezing, crystallisation and condensation normally decrease its entropy.

entries.topic: Carnot heat input from work output
entries.sourceReasonReference: The original names a Carnot engine and gives both reservoir temperatures and work output, so the heat-input calculation is defined. However, applying the efficiency relation numerically may exceed the Knowledge-level classification of the closest printed SLO.

entries.topic: ratio of Carnot efficiencies at two temperature pairs
entries.sourceReasonReference: Both temperature pairs define physically ordered hot and cold reservoirs above absolute zero, and the efficiency ratio is calculable. Correct treatment converts all Celsius values, including the negative Celsius value, to positive Kelvin temperatures; applying the formula twice requires teacher confirmation of its cognitive-level fit.

Work is the pressure-volume path integral and can differ for the listed processes. Calling one process universally maximum is not valid without specifying the same initial state, an appropriate common final volume, gas model, allowed paths and any other comparison constraints.

entries.topic: refrigerator COP from room and cabinet temperatures
entries.publisherStemConcern: unprovided room temperature and ideal reversible model for COP
entries.sourceReasonReference: The question says room temperature but gives no numerical hot-reservoir temperature. Furthermore a real refrigerator's COP does not equal the Carnot ideal by default; inferring cabinet temperature requires an explicit reversible Carnot assumption and hot temperature in kelvin.

entries.topic: efficiency change after doubling heat-source temperature
entries.publisherStemConcern: efficiency ratio lacks starting temperatures/unchanged sink assumptions
entries.sourceReasonReference: Even under a Carnot model with fixed cold reservoir, the new-to-old efficiency ratio depends on the original hot and cold temperatures. The question supplies neither initial temperatures nor a fixed cold-reservoir condition or instruction to double absolute kelvin temperature.

entries.topic: thermodynamics scope versus types of system
entries.publisherStemConcern: printed choices do not answer the requested definition
entries.sourceReasonReference: The question requests what thermodynamics studies, but the printed response choices describe various conditions of heat/mass transfer or dissipation. No printed option answers the stated subject-definition question; selecting a letter would conceal this source mismatch.

Equal temperature is the defining thermal-equilibrium criterion in the original source and the official outcome description. The framework prints P-12-C-01 within a Grade XI domain; never silently normalize to P-11-C-01.
entries.frameworkPrintedCodeAnomaly: P-12-C-01 in Grade XI domain; no unverified renumbering

entries.topic: isothermal pressure–volume figure and internal energy
entries.sourceReasonReference: The graph on p.151 is required evidence of an isothermal trajectory. A real substance can have internal-energy dependence on volume at constant temperature. The intended inference requires stating that the working substance behaves as an ideal gas; dropping the graph from a digital test also destroys necessary context.

entries.topic: internal energy as a path-independent state property
entries.publisherStemConcern: multiple endpoint-state energy analogies are defensible
entries.sourceReasonReference: For a fixed-mass system, kinetic energy depends on speed and gravitational potential energy in a conservative gravitational field depends on position. Both changes are endpoint-dependent, as is internal-energy change. Without restricting the intended comparison, the source offers more than one viable analogy.

The primary chapter establishes Avogadro's number using N_A. Another printed option uses a symbol resembling N_o or N_0; it has not been defined as synonymous in the checked pages. The source appears to have an intended distinct answer, but a digital recreation must not blur the subscripts.

entries.topic: thermal expansion of hollow and solid spheres
entries.presentationCompletenessRequirement: retain fourth printed answer option continued onto page 152
entries.sourceReasonReference: The question's last option continues onto p.152, so one-page extraction leaves the original four choices incomplete. Under uniform expansion of identical material and external dimensions, outer linear expansion does not depend on whether the sphere is hollow. The present Unit8 official domain inventory has no direct thermal-expansion row.

entries.topic: different thermal expansion rates across materials
entries.sourceReasonReference: The printed alternatives support a physically meaningful material-dependence principle. However, textbook placement alone does not establish the question as assessable under the confirmed Heat and Thermodynamics framework outcomes, which do not list thermal expansion separately.

The source asks why pressure rises after driving; this is common but not inevitable under all weather, inflation, heat-loss and driving conditions. A teacher note should say that air temperature generally rises owing to tyre deformation and dissipation, with volume approximately constant; qualitative pressure–temperature reasoning uses absolute pressure, not gauge pressure, if calculating.

During isothermal melting or vaporisation, absorbed latent heat increases intermolecular potential-energy contribution to internal energy while the substance temperature remains constant. This should not be conflated with the ideal-gas result that U depends only on T for a fixed amount of ideal gas.

entries.topic: temperature change in an isolated system
entries.sourceReasonReference: A blanket claim that an isolated system always has constant temperature is invalid: isolation blocks net matter/energy exchange with the surroundings, not internal transformations. Internal mechanical energy may dissipate into thermal energy without external work/heat; a portion can warm as other portions cool. The answer must specify the boundary, redistribution and relevant equilibrium assumptions.

entries.topic: distinguishing heat transfer and work from internal-energy change
entries.sourceReasonReference: The textbook's description of 'orderly macroscopic work' versus 'disorderly microscopic energy Q' is introductory language and may mislead if interpreted as distinct stored substances. Both Q and W are boundary energy transfers, and a measured ΔU does not uniquely reveal the split; independent information about a temperature-gradient transfer, force/displacement or other process mechanism is required. Apply the book's sign convention consistently.

entries.topic: double gas volume at fixed pressure
entries.sourceReasonReference: The question explicitly supplies an initial Celsius temperature, a doubled volume and constant pressure. Solving in Celsius without conversion incorrectly treats zero Celsius as absolute zero. The ideal-gas approximation, constant gas amount and kelvin conversion are implicit teaching assumptions. The calculation is numerically well defined but its Application demand is not automatically authorized by a printed Understanding-only candidate outcome.

entries.topic: whether heat input always raises internal energy
entries.sourceReasonReference: The word 'necessarily' must not be misread as an always-positive state-variable change. For a closed system with negligible kinetic/potential energy variation and the textbook's work-by convention, the first-law balance allows positive, zero or negative ΔU depending on the work done by the system. Avoid implying a heat input is stored completely as internal energy.

The original asks about a comparison that requires two curves evaluated at the same state, on the same P–V axes. The usual power laws rely on a reversible/quasistatic ideal-gas model (often constant heat capacities). Comparing slopes at unrelated points or asserting the result for arbitrary real fluids without conditions would be misleading. Cognitive and direct-SLO fit also need teacher sign-off.

entries.topic: typical rates of isothermal versus adiabatic processes
entries.sourceReasonReference: The original's 'typically' expresses a pedagogical heuristic, not a thermodynamic definition. Isothermal means constant temperature; adiabatic means no heat crosses the system boundary. The process rate alone does not establish either property, and the current source framework inventory has no confirmed direct SLO about rate as a definition.

entries.topic: whether a path can be adiabatic and isothermal
entries.sourceReasonReference: A categorical 'never' would be wrong, while a casual free-expansion example can also mislead by treating an irreversible non-equilibrium transient as a reversible isothermal curve. The explanation must state which temperatures and system boundaries are compared and make clear the limited assumptions of ideal-gas free expansion. Mapping to the printed First Law outcome is indirect.

entries.topic: entropy after a Carnot engine cycle
entries.sourceReasonReference: The wording asks whether entropy of a Carnot engine increases each cycle; a reply must distinguish the cyclic working fluid from the complete engine plus reservoirs, and must not equate individual reservoir entropy changes with total entropy generation. Reversible Carnot cycle and generic irreversible engine are different cases; the exact candidate SLO fit needs teacher review.

The original asks whether the entropy of 'a system' increases or decreases due to friction. For an isolated system, friction produces entropy, but without defining the system boundary and heat exchanges, the net system entropy change cannot be inferred from friction alone. A qualified response should preserve the common isolated-whole result without making an unbounded absolute claim.

The question is answerable as a qualitative compare/contrast: the central reversed-heat-engine mechanism is common, while the target region, purpose and often moisture control differ. Avoid claiming that air conditioning and food refrigeration necessarily use fundamentally different cycles; implementations may be identical in principle.

The original has (i) whether work is done on the coffee, (ii) whether coffee internal energy increases, (iii) whether its temperature rises and (iv) whether it receives outside heat. A digital or solved edition that drops a subpart or equates mechanical work with exterior heat is incomplete. The vessel is only approximately adiabatic and not all shaking work becomes coffee internal energy; a small rise may be below instrument resolution.

Original text p.129 states that temperature is directly proportional to gas-molecule mean kinetic energy and broadly says internal energy follows T, and p.130 says U does not change whenever temperature is constant. The blanket constant-T claim is not universal for real matter and phase changes, as the other original short question 8.2 itself illustrates. Keep the source framing, flag its ideal-gas/domain assumptions explicitly, and avoid deriving U=(3/2)nRT for all gases or all substances.

The short source prompt requests the gas laws generally, while the original chapter specifically organizes the topic under three named subsections on pp.134–135: Boyle, Charles and Gay-Lussac. An approved solution should follow these three first rather than import additional named laws as if printed in this section. Include which P,V,T variable is constant and any graph limits, and ensure any optional calculation or extended derivation is separately checked against printed SLO/cognitive demands.

The source on printed p.135 writes heat supplied to the system and work done by the system; switching mid-solution to work done on the gas flips the work sign. The requested explanation must preserve conservation and correctly distinguish internal-energy change from heat/work transfer. A general open-system energy balance cannot be silently treated as identical to the closed-system formula.

entries.presentationCompletenessRequirement: retain process-question subparts (a)–(d) in original order
entries.sourceReasonReference: Printed source Question 8.4 lists (a) isothermal, (b) isobaric, (c) adiabatic, (d) isochoric. The chapter's own teaching sequence is isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric, isobaric, so a careless extraction may reorder or omit a question part. The textbook's claim that ΔU=0 for an isothermal step must be scoped to an ideal gas; an isochoric process eliminates only PΔV boundary work; adiabatic does not mean 'necessarily rapid' or 'necessarily reversible.' Official outcome P-11-C-08 is broad, requiring further teacher scrutiny of this four-part coverage.

Original textbook pp.140–141 explains Figure 8.14 and writes W=Q1−Q2. A teacher answer must label heat input and heat rejected as positive magnitudes and must not treat W as the net result for any arbitrary noncyclic step, where ΔU may be nonzero. The source's 'every heat engine must have three parts' is a useful idealised schematic; a modern open-system internal-combustion engine should not be represented as literally identical to a closed working-fluid Carnot loop. The claimed historical priority of Carnot as 'first heat engine' is outside the requested physics mechanism and should not be repeated as independently verified history.

The original source printed p.142 labels the statements as Lord Kelvin and Rudolf Clausius and phrases the first as single-reservoir heat fully converted to work while 'no change' remains in the working system. Without the essential cyclic-and-sole-result condition, students may wrongly conclude that no heat can ever be converted completely into work during a finite noncyclic transformation. Clausius likewise does not prohibit refrigerated cold-to-hot transfer when external work supplies a compensating effect. Preserve the publisher question and distinguish these as equivalent formulations of one Second Law rather than two independent principles.

entries.presentationCompletenessRequirement: independently verify four Carnot steps and references to Figures 8.16–8.17 before a diagram explanation
entries.sourceReasonReference: Original pp.143–145 give the four steps, original Figures 8.16 and 8.17, Eq. 8.8 for net cycle work and Eq. 8.9 for Carnot efficiency. The source says broadly 'heat Q is proportional to absolute temperature T' before substituting the temperature ratio; this must be read specifically as a ratio for the reversible heat exchanges of the Carnot cycle, not as universal Q∝T. The printed p.144 'Do You Know?' box distinguishes ideal- versus real-gas internal energy and cannot justify arbitrary real-gas isothermal ΔU=0. The original question requests defining/explaining Carnot's engine and its efficiency relation; an authentic derivation and labelled curve should be explained carefully, but no copied publisher figure or unapproved answer edition may be published. The secondary printed outcome P-11-C-23 is Knowledge while this derived calculation and step explanation can be Application-level.

The original textbook pp.145–147 describes a refrigerator as a reversed heat engine, illustrates Figure 8.18 and uses work input together with cold-side heat and hot-side rejected heat. Page 146 then introduces a temperature-based COP immediately after saying heat is proportional to absolute temperature; that proportionality is NOT a general refrigerator law. Temperature ratios can be used only for reversible Carnot heat exchanges, with kelvin temperatures; a real compressor has losses. An eventual response to 'explain working' should prioritize the physically correct heat/work flow rather than copying the generalization as universal. Do not conflate food refrigeration with the room-heating COP of a heat pump.

Textbook p.147 prints ΔS=ΔQ/T following a reversible-process assumption but risks making the formula look universal. Page 148 explicitly says melting ice releases heat and its entropy decreases, despite the same page's ice-to-water order/disorder figure and the source's worked Example 8.6 on p.149, which correctly gives a positive ΔS for melting. Page 149 further says entropy of the SYSTEM remains constant in all reversible processes, which is false for reversible heat transfer or phase change: it is total entropy generation of system plus surroundings that vanishes for a reversible overall process. Keep the original exercise question but explicitly flag these exact contradictory publisher passages before any teacher answer edition.

Source p.149 writes that only processes with a nondecreasing system entropy are natural, that for all reversible processes system entropy stays constant, that entropy increases in any irreversible process, and that all heat of a car-engine process was available for work before degradation. These statements are too broad for subsystems, ideal reversibility and real thermal conversion constraints. Clarify the entropy balance of the ISOLATED total and the loss of useful-work potential (exergy), not disappearance of energy. Page 148's arrowed high-disorder-to-low-disorder sketch (Figure 8.20) should be independently checked before use in a student explanation; no publisher figure is copied into this review.

A numerical result can be reproduced only after selecting a reference temperature for 'room temperature' and interpreting the stated 180 kPa as absolute. About 293–303 K yields approximately 0.309–0.299 mol and rounds to 0.3 mol at one decimal. Balloon pressure is often reported as gauge pressure outside this exercise; the ideal-gas formula needs absolute pressure. Preserve original radius 10 cm exactly and convert cubic centimetres to cubic metres implicitly by converting radius first.

entries.topic: heat engine between water fixed points
entries.sourceReasonReference: Temperature difference by itself is insufficient to determine actual efficiency of an arbitrary heat engine. The printed answer is the ideal Carnot upper bound. Both the implicit reversibility condition and the cognitive level matter: using the symbolic ideal-efficiency equation numerically is Application, while the closest official P-11-C-23 outcome is recorded as Knowledge. Keep the source question and printed answer unchanged, but do not promote the result as universal without explicitly stating the model.

entries.topic: gas volume change after 1 K increase
entries.publisherStemConcern: missing initial numerical T and process/constant-P condition
entries.sourceReasonReference: The printed source does not give an initial numerical temperature and does not state constant pressure. Its answer of 0.37 m³ appears to assume both constant pressure and approximately 273 K, yet neither condition is present in the question stem. These are two distinct missing inputs/assumptions and cannot be repaired by rounding or by treating 'pressure P' as 'pressure kept at P'. Do not publish a single teacher key or alter the publisher question; seek teacher endorsement of a separately authored, fully specified practice variant.

entries.topic: Carnot engine work and stated absorption temperature
entries.publisherStemConcern: printed low-reservoir heat absorption contradicts heat-engine result
entries.sourceReasonReference: Original printed p.153 explicitly says the Carnot engine absorbs 600 J of heat at the low temperature of 400 K, although the high-temperature reservoir is 600 K. Using 600 J as high-side input changes the source meaning and gives 200 J, the publisher answer. In a reversed Carnot refrigerator absorbing 600 J from 400 K, the input work would instead be 300 J. If 600 J were heat rejected to 400 K from an engine, its reversible work would also be 300 J. These are distinct devices and transfers; preserve the publisher conflict rather than relabel the source as correct.

Original p.153 gives 220 W, 136 g water, initial 23.5 °C, and asks time to bring it to the boiling point while ignoring heat loss. It does not supply the numerical value of specific heat capacity. Assuming ordinary water boils at 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure gives ΔT=76.5 K; with c=4186 J/(kg K), t≈197.96 s and printed 198 s. With c=4200, t≈198.62 s, a one-second rounded difference. Do not confuse bringing water to its boiling point with vaporizing it, which would require latent heat.

The source says 'a heat engine at room temperature' has 50% efficiency and asks the difference between two heat source temperatures after efficiency becomes 70%. It does not numerically define room temperature and does not explicitly name an ideal reversible Carnot engine with a fixed cold reservoir. The Carnot formula η=1−T_C/T_H at the same cold temperature implies ΔT_H=(4/3)T_C, yielding ≈397.33 K if T_C=298 K, consistent with its 397 K printed result. At T_C=300 K the same formula gives 400 K, so the printed answer is assumption-specific, not an unqualified general result.

The original question explicitly identifies a Carnot engine, names heat absorbed Q at temperature T, and gives a cold reservoir T/3. The reversible Carnot relationship therefore implies Q_C/Q_H=(T/3)/T=1/3, reproducing the publisher's Q/3. Q_C denotes the POSITIVE MAGNITUDE of rejected heat; the signed heat transferred to the working substance on the cold isotherm is −Q/3. A general irreversible heat engine does not obey this exact heat ratio. The printed SLO P-11-C-23 is Knowledge but computing a symbolic heat ratio is an Application task, so teacher mapping remains pending.

Original p.153 supplies 500 J to melt 2 g at 0°C, then asks for the entropy change of 70 g of water at 0°C when it freezes in a refrigerator. This fixes a source-specific latent energy of 250 J/g, which should not be replaced with a standard tabulated fusion value. Freezing reverses melting, so heat Q for the water is negative, −500(70/2)=−17,500 J, and ΔS of the WATER is −17,500/273.15≈−64.07 J/K. The printed −64 J K⁻¹ is consistent after rounding. This does not establish the total refrigerator+room entropy balance; no direct summative entropy-numerical SLO has been authenticated in original V224 Domain C.

entries.presentationCompletenessRequirement: retain BOTH (a) numeric work and (b) an independently validated labeled P–V diagram
entries.sourceReasonReference: Printed original Numerical 8.9 has TWO explicit subparts: (a) calculate work done BY gas from 1 m³ to 2 m³ at constant atmospheric pressure, and (b) represent the work on a PV diagram. Using 1 atm≈1.013×10⁵ Pa, ΔV=+1 m³, W_by=PΔV=+1.013×10⁵ J matches the printed value. At the more exact 101325 Pa the answer is 101325 J, rounding consistently. A complete marking scheme needs a labeled P–V plot with a rightward horizontal isobar and area below it between the two volumes; a numerical answer alone fails the printed part (b). The pressure/volume model treats the gas expansion as quasistatic against the stated constant ambient pressure.
